codes.construct: Cambridge Dialogue Analysis Scheme (CDAS): 13 dialogic move categories in classroom talk (e.g., reasoning, invitations for reasoning, other invitation, agreement, elaboration). These are educational discourse codes, so they may not count as a psychological construct.
codes.texts: Transcribed classroom dialogue: 1,386 coded teacher–student turns from three UK primary school lessons (one English, two mathematics); 55-turn sets were used for the human–AI collaboration conditions.
codes.models: Customised GPT Coding Assistant (CGCA), an OpenAI custom GPT, apparently GPT-4-based (the exact version is not stated), refined through several prompt iterations.
codes.human_reference: Original CDAS project coders (trained coders) who coded the same turns ("comparing its codes with those generated in the project").
codes.human_human_agreement: The paper cites 70–75% inter-coder agreement from the original CDAS study, which may not be on the same units. It also reports human coder vs CDAS reference Cohen's κ: baseline 0.112–0.337; Condition A mean ≈ .40; Condition B mean ≈ .45 (B was AI-assisted).

agreement_stats.configuration: Final refined prompt (decision-tree logic, curated examples)
agreement_stats.quote: the final AI assistant achieved 64.9% turn-level precision, approaching the 70–75% inter-coder agreement reported in the original CDAS study
the baseline CGCA performed with precision across codes ranged from 6.7% to 38.2%, indicating limited alignment with human annotations

codes.note: An LLM codes turns against human CDAS codes, with turn-level precision reported. Doubt is I2: CDAS dialogic moves are educational, not clearly psychological (E3 if excluded). Precision is the only LLM-alone statistic. Table 2 κ compares human coders (with or without AI help) to the reference, not the LLM alone. Prompts and appendices are in supplementary files not received.

codes.construct: Factual accuracy of autism-related informational statements (inaccurate / overgeneralized / accurate) judged against current scientific knowledge, i.e. health misinformation grading rather than a psychological construct of the writer
codes.texts: 408 Italian informational statements extracted from manual transcripts of 148 TikTok videos posted under #Autismo
codes.models: ChatGPT 4.0 mini; Gemini 1.5 Flash (zero-shot, Italian prompt, one chat session per statement)
codes.human_reference: Three clinical experts in autism (co-authors), working independently and blinded; the median of their three ratings was used as ground truth
codes.human_human_agreement: Pairwise weighted Cohen's kappa 0.40–0.64, mean 0.52 (p.4); specific positive agreement by pair: accurate 0.81–0.90, overgeneralization 0.46–0.69, inaccurate 0.17–0.79 (Table 1)

agreement_stats.quote: whereas Gemini 1.5 Flash reached only fair agreement (κ = 0.29)

codes.note: Borderline. The scheme grades whether autism health claims are factually accurate (misinformation, E3). It does not code the writer's mental states. If judged clinical, it would be T1 and eligible with the statistics above. Table 4's caption says ChatGPT, but the rows are Gemini. Accuracy is not printed; from the matrices, ChatGPT 308/408 and Gemini 291/408.

codes.construct: Suicide risk level of help-seekers (non-SR, global suicide risk, imminent suicide risk)
codes.texts: About 17,000 labelled Hebrew online crisis-chat conversations between help-seekers and counsellors (Sahar service, 2017–2022)
codes.models: Only encoder models: SR-BERT (hierarchical, based on AlephBERT/DialogBERT), IMSR-BERT, Ensemble SI-BERT, plus XGBoost and Doc2Vec baselines. No generative LLM.
codes.human_reference: Labels from Sahar volunteer counsellors; a sample of 500 conversations was validated by clinical psychologists who specialise in suicide
codes.human_human_agreement: Krippendorff's α = 0.766 between the psychologists and the counsellor SR label on 500 conversations (p. 5)
codes.possible_duplicate: This is an extended version of Izmaylov et al. (2023), "Combining psychological theory with language models for suicide risk detection", Findings of EACL 2023. It is related to Bialer et al. (2022, COLING) and Grimland et al. (2024).
codes.note: The title says 'large language models', but every model is BERT-based (encoder) or classical ML. The limitations section states: "we did not use generative models (such as ChatGPT) in this research due to privacy considerations" (p. 21). Recall, precision, F1 and F2 against the counsellor labels are reported for these encoder models only (Tables 2, 5 and 6).

codes.construct: Safety of chatbot responses to suicide risk on the VERA-MH rubric. There are 5 dimensions: detects risk, confirms risk, guides to human care, supportive conversation, follows AI boundaries. Each is rated best practice / suboptimal / high potential for harm / not relevant.
codes.texts: 90 simulated multiturn conversations between LLM user-agents (simulated users at different suicide risk levels) and general-purpose chatbots (GPT-4o, GPT-5.0, Gemini 3), giving 450 conversation-dimensions.
codes.models: LLM judges: GPT-4o (primary), GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Flash. Each was prompted with the same item text as the clinician rating form.
codes.human_reference: 6 licensed clinicians (2 clinical psychologists, 4 counselors/MFTs); 3 rated each conversation. References were the clinician consensus (modal rating) and the expert (psychologist) rating.
codes.human_human_agreement: Clinician-clinician Krippendorff alpha (nominal) = 0.77 (95% CI 0.71-0.82) across the 6 clinicians, over 90 conversations x 5 dimensions.

agreement_stats.configuration: LLM judge vs clinician consensus, overall across dimensions
agreement_stats.quote: LLM-clinician IRR (GPT-4o as judge) | LLM and clinician consensus | 0.81 (0.75-0.87)
LLM-clinician IRR (GPT-5.2 as judge) | LLM and clinician consensus | 0.78 (0.71-0.85)
LLM-clinician IRR (Sonnet 4.5 as judge) | LLM and clinician consensus | 0.82 (0.75-0.87)
LLM-clinician IRR (Gemini 2.5 Flash as judge) | LLM and clinician consensus | 0.77 (0.70-0.84)

agreement_stats.configuration: LLM as additional rater alongside all individual clinicians
agreement_stats.quote: When treating the LLM judge (GPT-4o) as an additional rater alongside the clinician raters, IRR was 0.76 (95% CI 0.71-0.81)

agreement_stats.configuration: vs clinician consensus, stratified: GPT-4o provider-agent conversations
agreement_stats.quote: LLM-clinician IRR was the highest when evaluating conversations with GPT-4o as the provider-agent (LLM vs clinician consensus=0.92, 95% CI 0.87-0.96)

agreement_stats.configuration: vs clinician consensus, stratified: Gemini 3 provider-agent conversations
agreement_stats.quote: lowest for conversations with Gemini 3 (IRR=0.71, 95% CI 0.59-0.81)

agreement_stats.configuration: Sensitivity for 'high potential for harm' vs clinician consensus
agreement_stats.quote: Sensitivity for assigning "high potential for harm" across the LLM judges... ranged from 77.4% (82/106, Sonnet 4.5)

agreement_stats.configuration: Sensitivity for 'high potential for harm' vs clinician consensus

codes.possible_duplicate: Possibly overlaps with the original VERA-MH proposal paper (ref [14], which may be an arXiv preprint) and with any preprint version of this validation study.
codes.note: T4: LLM judges and clinicians apply the same suicide-safety rubric to the same simulated conversations. Alphas are nominal, pooled over 5 dimensions. Dimension-level and stratified IRR, raw agreement and confusion matrices are in Appendices 3, 5 and 9, which are not in the text. LLM–LLM alphas (0.73–0.98) are also reported.

codes.construct: Quality of chatbot refusal responses to high-risk prompts (suicide/self-harm, substance use, violence, weapons, sexual crimes): refusal (yes/no), psychological grounding (1–5), external resource referral (yes/no), relevance/tailoring (1–5)
codes.texts: 50 assistant responses (Qwen 3.5 27B with v0 and v1 system prompts) to 25 harmful prompts from safety benchmarks, 5 per risk cluster
codes.models: LLM judges: Qwen 3.5 397B-A17B, GLM 4.7, Mistral Large 3 675B Instruct
codes.human_reference: One human annotator (student assistant studying business informatics, Appendix N; called "human expert" in main text) rated the same 50 responses on the same 4 criteria

agreement_stats.quote: Qwen 3.5 397B-A17B is the judge with the highest agreement with the human expert, with κ = 0.61
and finally Mistral Large 3 675B Instruct with κ = 0.56

codes.note: T4 judge-selection substudy (50 responses) inside a paper on refusal design. Psychological construct mainly in C2 (psychological grounding); refusal/relevance less so. Table 10 gives per-criterion and per-version (v0/v1) Pearson, Spearman, % agreement and kappa. Human rater is a business informatics student despite being called an "expert". SORRY-Bench/XSTest judges are not checked against humans.
